conservation.notes: IUCN Red List category from Wikidata P141 (least concern, Q211005); the English article cites BirdLife International (2025) for LC.

human_tolerance.notes: Breeders need quiet wetland territories and are easily disturbed (German article: disturbance in breeding territories); the English article says it has adapted to human settlement in many areas. Nests on farmland near wetlands are reported by Gicquel et al. 2026.

phases.name: spawning_migration
phases.note: Return from wintering quarters. The German article reports that cranes now return to central Europe as early as February. The DE activity curve rises in February (0.75 of peak) and is at its highest in October and November.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Two eggs are usually laid from March to mid-April in Central Europe; incubation lasts about 30 to 31 days (German article).

phases.name: young
phases.note: Chicks hatch from spring and become able to fly after about ten weeks (German article); families gather at staging sites from late July onward.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Large resting groups arrive on the German lowlands from mid-August and feed on stubble until the autumn migration (German article: staging from mid-September, departure in autumn).

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Most German-breeding cranes winter in Iberia and France. The German article notes rare overwintering in Germany, which is not modelled here. The DE curve is lowest in January (0.13 of peak). Fraction not stated.

vocalizations.description: A loud, piercing trumpeting call given in flight and during display. It carries a considerable distance; the long coiled trachea gives it the trumpet quality.

A paired double call, given as a warning when disturbed. One bird calls with its neck stretched forward, and the partner answers with a deeper or higher note. It is often heard over long distances in disturbed breeding territories.

conservation.note: IUCN category from Wikidata P141 (Q211005, least concern); the English article cites BirdLife International (2025).

range.note: Country list assembled from named breeding countries in Gicquel et al. 2026 section 2.2 (Germany, Finland, Sweden, Norway, Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania, Czech Republic, France, Spain), the English article (Denmark, Netherlands, Slovakia, European Russia, Turkey, Israel, Iraq, Iran, Pakistan, India, Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand, China, Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Tunisia, Portugal) and the German article (Belarus, Ukraine omitted: not named as breeding in the cited passages). Extirpated breeders (Italy, Hungary) are excluded.

range.introduced.note: The English article describes an ongoing reintroduction in the United Kingdom, and Gicquel et al. include UK-reintroduced birds.

traits.limb_count.note: Two legs; wings are not counted under the schema convention.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk: the German article describes feeding on foot on meadows and stubble and walking in straight lines and curves during display; Fly: migration flocks in flight (English article). Glide is not used by any action in the program.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Bird; endothermy is the default for birds.

traits.flight.note: Powered flight on migration and in display.

traits.metamorphosis.note: No larval metamorphosis, as for birds generally.

traits.nest_type.note: German article: 'Kraniche sind Bodenbrüter'; the nest is built on a platform of plant material in shallow water, 10 to 20 cm above the surface, which maps to Ground.

traits.perching.note: Authored judgement: cranes roost in shallow water and forage on the ground, and neither source describes perching in trees.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (5.4 kg is Medium: under 50 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: English article: 'body weight can range from 3 to 6.1 kg, with the nominate subspecies averaging around 5.4 kg'. The nominate subspecies is the European form. The value is not a captive figure.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: English article: 3 to 6.1 kg across the species.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the English article's 100 to 130 cm length range.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of the English article's 180 to 240 cm wingspan range.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Proxy: life expectancy at birth of 10 years (Gicquel et al. 2026 abstract; 10.5 years in section 3.5). It is a period mean from a 1985-2021 survival model of 5049 banded cranes, not a typical adult lifespan. The paper's maximum (25 years) and captive figures are not used. Disagreement: the English article cites a Euring-based elementary estimate of about 5 years at birth, and says wild longevity data are expected to be updated. The value follows the preflight directive and the peer-reviewed estimate.

traits.diet.note: Authored allocation. Gicquel et al. 2026 section 2.1: plants (rhizomes, roots, leaves, berries, seeds, cereals), plus invertebrates, and occasionally amphibians, reptiles, rodents and birds. The English article: plant matter largely, waste grain in winter, animal foods more important in summer. The German article: seeds in spring staging, insects and small vertebrates in early summer. Browse covers leaves, stems and tubers; fruit covers berries. The percentages are judgement, not measured diet shares.

traits.social.note: English article: flocks of up to 400 in migration, small groups for foraging and roosting. German article: breeding pairs are solitary on their territories in summer, and the rest of the year is spent in groups.

traits.activity_pattern.note: German article: roosting overnight in shallow water, calling at first light, leaving around sunrise, feeding through the day and returning in the evening.

traits.defense.note: Authored judgement from the German article's description of warning calls and disturbance sensitivity. Cranes leave when disturbed rather than hiding or freezing.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement, not measured: the German article describes high disturbance sensitivity in breeding territories and flocks that watch for danger. The value is 0.7.

habitat.use.note: Authored time-budget allocation between feeding on land, roosting and feeding in shallow wetland, and flying.

habitat.resources.note: Seed use is limited to months with stubble and staging (August to November, February to April). Invertebrates are used all year. Water roosts and nest sites are on shallow water and ground in wetlands.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Roost in shallow water: the German article says the cranes sleep overnight in shallow water at their roosting sites. The tag 'water' is the nearest available resource tag.

habitat.requires.note: Authored placement rule: water within 1000 m. Supported by the German article's shallow-water roosts and wetland nest sites and by Gicquel et al.'s wetland breeding habitat. The distance is judgement, not measured.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Authored judgement from adaptation to farmland and settlements (English article and Gicquel) and disturbance sensitivity in breeding territories (German article). Urban affinity is set to Adapter.

seasonal.note: Phases apply to region DE only. Dates come from the German article: return in February, laying March to mid-April, incubation 30 to 31 days, fledging about ten weeks, staging from mid-August, and wintering elsewhere. Other regions are not modelled.

behavior.note: Species-local program bt-crane-wetland-forager-v1 (see behavior.json). Night roost in shallow water, dawn calls, flight from threats to water, feeding on stubble and invertebrates on foot, and ground nesting in March to June.

vocalizations.trumpet.note: English article: loud trumpeting call given in flight and display, audible from a considerable distance. German article: loud trumpeting flight calls with a resonance chamber in the 100 to 130 cm trachea.

vocalizations.alarm_pair.note: German article: the double call is started by one bird with its neck stretched; the partner follows with a deeper or higher note. It is used in warnings and heard over long distances in disturbed breeding territories.

look.note: Authored block-mesh judgement (taller legs, long neck, slate-grey body, black head and bill, red crown patch, drooping tertial plume). No source measures the mesh.
